summary: This note is a collection of extracted passages from the Wikipedia article on Neptune, covering its discovery dispute, orbit, weather, rings, size and position in the Solar System, and its relationship to the Kuiper belt. It notes that Le Verrier and Adams were jointly credited with the discovery after nationalistic rivalry, and describes Neptune's orbital period, storm systems, atmospheric temperatures and ring structure. Several passages repeat or overlap, so some facts appear more than once.
one_line: Wikipedia-derived notes on Neptune's discovery credit, orbit, extreme winds, rings, size, and role bordering the Kuiper belt.
key_facts: Neptune orbits the Sun on average every 164.79 years at an average distance of about 30.1 AU (4.5 billion km).
On 11 July 2011, Neptune completed its first full barycentric orbit since its discovery in 1846.
Neptune is 17 times the mass of Earth and is slightly more massive than its near-twin Uranus, which is 15 times the mass of Earth.
Winds on Neptune have been recorded reaching almost 600 m/s (2,200 km/h; 1,300 mph), nearly reaching supersonic flow.
At cloud tops, prevailing winds range from 400 m/s along the equator to 250 m/s at the poles.
In 2007, the upper troposphere of Neptune's south pole was found to be about 10 K warmer than the rest of its atmosphere, which averages approximately 73 K.

Neptune's ring system is much less substantial than that of Saturn; its three main rings are the Adams Ring at 63,000 km, the Le Verrier Ring at 53,000 km, and the Galle Ring at 42,000 km from Neptune's centre.
Neptune is named after the Roman god of the sea and its astronomical symbol is a stylised version of the god's trident.
Because of its distance from Earth, Neptune's angular diameter ranges only from 2.2 to 2.4 arcseconds, the smallest of the Solar System planets.
The Kuiper belt extends from Neptune's orbit at 30 AU out to about 55 AU from the Sun, and Neptune's gravity dominates its structure.
Neptune was the farthest known planet from its discovery in 1846 until the discovery of Pluto in 1930.
In 2006, the International Astronomical Union reclassified Pluto as a 'dwarf planet', making Neptune once again the outermost known planet.
During the Voyager 2 flyby in 1989, Neptune's southern hemisphere had a Great Dark Spot comparable to the Great Red Spot on Jupiter.
In 2004 and 2005, five new small satellites of Neptune with diameters between 38 and 61 kilometres were discovered.
In 1998 the 'Neptune papers' returned to the Royal Observatory, Greenwich, and historians concluded that Adams does not deserve equal credit with Le Verrier for the discovery.
